papers.title: Cruella: A Unified Microscaling and Floating-Point Dot-Product Unit for LLM Inference on FPGAs
authors: Jinho Yang, Taehyeong Kim, Mincheol Cha, Hyeoncheol Kim, Donggeun Kim, Nahye Kim, Yujin Lee, Ryeowook Ko, Woong Gyu Park, Jiwoong Park, Junsoo Kim, Tae-Hyoung Kim, Yongjun Park, Seongmin Hong, Joo-Young Kim
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2611.27323v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The number formats that accelerators execute natively are fixed at fabrication, yet large language model (LLM) checkpoints are released with MXFP4 weights in the Microscaling (MX) formats standardized in 2023. FPGAs adopt new formats through bitstreams. However, to the best of our knowledge, no deployed FPGA LLM accelerator executes MXFP4 weights alongside BF16 products. We characterize the decoding of MXFP4 checkpoints, whose layers alternate between MXFP4$\times$BF16 products and BF16$\times$BF16 products of attention and BF16 layers. With a BF16 KV cache, BF16$\times$BF16 products take 56%-77% of the datapath time, during which a separate MXFP4 unit idles. papers.title: Mind the Delta: Early Pruning of RTL Variants for Agentic Hardware Optimization
authors: Siyang Cai, Cangyuan Li, Haoyu Gao, Kun Wang, Mochen Li, Yilin Zhong, Ke Xu, Yinhe Han, Ying Wang
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2611.27035v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous coding agents powered by large language models (LLMs) now write diverse microarchitectural variants of existing register-transfer level (RTL) designs at high throughput, shifting the primary bottleneck of agentic RTL optimization onto logic synthesis. Commercial toolchains take hours per variant, creating an acute compute asymmetry between proposing and evaluating variants. Existing fast evaluators falter in this regime. Subtle RTL edits trigger nonlinear synthesis shifts that learned predictors and coding agents cannot resolve, while synthesis proxies at reduced effort either alter the optimization trajectory or retain most of its runtime. papers.title: Can Language Models See the Circuit in Pixelated RFIC Passives?
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2611.27559v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The emergence of inverse-designed, pixelated passives for microwave and millimeter-wave applications has been a major development in the field of RFIC design. These devices, which appear to be QR-code-like in structure, exist in a generalizable, high-dimensional design space that includes conventional passive topologies. However, these structures are naturally unintuitive for designers, and failures or deviations in performance are difficult to debug. In this work, we ask whether a frontier language model can understand, predict, and edit the responses and layout structure of pixelated passives.
